traditions/christian-science/summary: Founded in Boston in 1879 by Mary Baker Eddy, raised a New England Congregationalist, following her recovery from injury in 1866 and her book Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (1875). It teaches that God is wholly good, infinite Mind, and that matter, sin and disease are not ultimately real, so healing comes through spiritual understanding rather than medicine. It reinterprets the Trinity and stands outside historic Nicene Christianity. It published the Christian Science Monitor (1908).
traditions/christian-science/distinctive: Spiritual healing through prayer and Christian Science practitioners
Science and Health as the "pastor" alongside the Bible
No ordained clergy; readers lead services
traditions/christian-science/profile/aut: The Bible and Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures as the impersonal pastor.
traditions/christian-science/profile/sal: Salvation as awakening from the belief in matter, sin and death through understanding of God as Mind and Love.
traditions/christian-science/profile/sac: Baptism and communion understood spiritually, without water or elements.
traditions/christian-science/profile/esc: Salvation realised through spiritual progress; no physical second coming emphasis.
traditions/christian-science/profile/gov: The Mother Church governed by a Board of Directors under the Church Manual.
traditions/christian-science/profile/wor: Sunday Lesson-Sermons read from the Bible and Science and Health; Wednesday testimony meetings.
traditions/christian-science/profile/can: The Bible with Science and Health.
traditions/christian-science/status: Active but much declined since the mid-twentieth century.
traditions/unity-church/name: Unity (Unity Church / Unity School of Christianity)
traditions/unity-church/summary: A New Thought movement founded in Kansas City in 1889 by Charles and Myrtle Fillmore after Myrtle's healing, influenced by Emma Curtis Hopkins (a former student of Mary Baker Eddy). Unity teaches the divinity in every person, affirmative prayer and the power of thought; it is known for the Silent Unity prayer ministry and the Daily Word. It stands outside historic Christian orthodoxy.
traditions/unity-church/distinctives/3: Jesus as the great example of the indwelling Christ
traditions/unity-church/profile/authorit: Scripture read metaphysically, with spiritual experience.
traditions/unity-church/profile/salvatio: Realisation of the Christ within; no doctrine of eternal punishment.
traditions/unity-church/profile/sacramen: No formal sacraments; symbolic baptism and communion in some congregations.
traditions/unity-church/profile/eschatol: Present spiritual realisation; reincarnation accepted by many.
traditions/unity-church/profile/governan: Unity Worldwide Ministries association of congregations; Unity World Headquarters at Unity Village.
traditions/shakers/name: Shakers (United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing)
traditions/shakers/summary: Emerged about 1747 near Manchester among followers of James and Jane Wardley, influenced by Quakers and French Camisard prophets. Ann Lee led a group to America in 1774; under Joseph Meacham and Lucy Wright the Shakers built celibate communal villages from Maine to Kentucky. Many Believers regarded Ann Lee as the female appearing of the Christ spirit. Known for ecstatic dance, gender equality in leadership, craftsmanship and songs like 'Simple Gifts'. Only Sabbathday Lake, Maine, remains, with a handful of members.
traditions/shakers/profile/authority: Scripture with ongoing revelation and the testimony of Ann Lee and early leaders.
traditions/shakers/profile/salvation: Salvation through confession, celibacy and a life of separation from the world.
traditions/shakers/profile/eschatology: Christ's second appearing understood as already begun in the Believers.
traditions/shakers/profile/governance: Ministry of elders and eldresses in each family and a central ministry.
traditions/shakers/profile/worship: Song and dance, later quieter meetings.
traditions/shakers/status: Nearly extinct: one community at Sabbathday Lake, Maine.
traditions/swedenborgian-new-church/summ: Churches based on the visionary writings of the Swedish scientist Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772), who taught that the Last Judgment occurred in the spiritual world in 1757 and that the Lord had opened the inner sense of Scripture. The first New Church society was organised in London in 1787. Swedenborgians teach that God is one in essence and person, Jesus Christ, in whom there is a trinity of love, wisdom and operation, rather than three persons; they therefore stand outside Nicene Trinitarianism as historically defined.
traditions/swedenborgian-new-church/dist: Revelation through Swedenborg of the spiritual sense of the Word
One God in one Person, the Lord Jesus Christ
Life of charity as essential to salvation
Detailed teaching on heaven, hell and the spiritual world
Influence on figures such as Blake, Emerson and Helen Keller
traditions/swedenborgian-new-church/prof: The Word in its spiritual sense, as unfolded in Swedenborg's Writings.
Regeneration through faith joined to charity and useful life; no vicarious satisfaction.
The Last Judgment occurred in 1757; the Second Coming is the revelation of the inner sense of Scripture; the New Jerusalem is descending.
Several bodies: General Conference (UK), General Convention (US, 1817) and the episcopally led General Church (Bryn Athyn).
The 'Word' as Swedenborg defined it (books with an internal sense), with the other biblical books valued as edifying.
traditions/bible-students/summary: Fellowships that continue Charles Taze Russell's original Bible Student movement (from 1879) and separated from the Watch Tower Society after J. F. Rutherford took control in 1917. Bodies such as the Pastoral Bible Institute (1918) and the Dawn Bible Students remain loyal to Russell's Studies in the Scriptures, rejecting Rutherford's centralisation. They share the movement's non-Trinitarian theology and stand outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
traditions/bible-students/distinctives/1: Ransom and restitution: a future opportunity for all humanity
traditions/bible-students/distinctives/2: Rejection of eternal torment and the Trinity
traditions/bible-students/profile/author: Scripture, read through Russell's Studies in the Scriptures.
traditions/bible-students/profile/salvat: Salvation through the ransom of Christ; most of humanity will receive an opportunity in the Millennial age.
traditions/bible-students/profile/sacram: Immersion of consecrated believers and the annual Memorial of Christ's death.
traditions/bible-students/profile/eschat: Millennial restitution of mankind on earth; a heavenly 'little flock' of 144,000.
traditions/bible-students/profile/worshi: Bible studies, testimony meetings and conventions.
traditions/church-of-god-seventh-day/sum: Sabbath-keeping Adventists, led initially by Gilbert Cranmer in Michigan (1858), who declined to follow Ellen G. White's prophetic authority or the name 'Seventh-day Adventist'. Organised as a General Conference in 1884 and later based in Denver, it experienced a 1933 schism (Salem, West Virginia). Historically non-Trinitarian (often binitarian), with views varying among its bodies; Herbert W. Armstrong came from its Oregon conference.
traditions/church-of-god-seventh-day/dis: Rejection of Ellen G. White's writings as authoritative
Annual Lord's Supper on Passover evening
Name "Church of God" as the biblical name
traditions/church-of-god-seventh-day/pro: Salvation by grace through faith, with obedience to God's commandments including the Sabbath.
Baptism by immersion and the annual Lord's Supper with feet washing.
Premillennial return of Christ; resurrection and annihilation of the wicked.
traditions/worldwide-church-of-god/summa: Founded as the Radio Church of God in 1933 in Eugene, Oregon, by Herbert W. Armstrong, a former Church of God (Seventh Day) minister, later headquartered in Pasadena with Ambassador College and The Plain Truth magazine. It taught Sabbath and Old Testament holy days, tithing, British Israelism and a binitarian 'God Family' that believers would join. After Armstrong's death it renounced these teachings (1993–97) and became Grace Communion International in 2009.
traditions/worldwide-church-of-god/disti: Seventh-day Sabbath and annual holy days
Mass media evangelism (The World Tomorrow broadcast)
traditions/worldwide-church-of-god/profi: Scripture as interpreted by Armstrong as God's apostle.
Obedience to God's law with Christ's sacrifice; believers to be born into the God Family at the resurrection.
Imminent end-time tribulation and the World Tomorrow.
traditions/worldwide-church-of-god/statu: Historic as described; transformed into Grace Communion International, while splinter groups continue Armstrong's teaching.
traditions/grace-communion-international: The former Worldwide Church of God, which under Joseph W. Tkach and his son Joseph Tkach Jr. rejected Armstrong's distinctive teachings, embraced the Trinity and salvation by grace, joined the National Association of Evangelicals (1997) and took a new name in 2009. Its theology is now strongly 'Trinitarian-incarnational', drawing on Karl Barth and T. F. and J. B. Torrance.
Salvation by grace without Old Covenant law
Scripture, read in harmony with the historic creeds.
Salvation by grace through Christ, who has included humanity in his life with the Father in the Spirit.
Christ's return and the reconciliation of all things in him; universalism not taught as dogma.
traditions/messianic-judaism/summary: A movement of Jewish people (and non-Jewish associates) who believe Jesus (Yeshua) is the Messiah while retaining Jewish identity and practice. It grew from nineteenth-century Hebrew Christian associations; the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America (1915) renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America in 1975, and the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations followed in 1979. Mainstream Jewish bodies and Israeli courts generally do not regard Messianic Jews as Jews, and many see the movement as a form of Christian missionising; Messianic Jews regard faith in Yeshua as the fulfilment of Judaism.
traditions/messianic-judaism/distinctive: Observance of Sabbath and Jewish festivals
Jewish identity affirmed after faith in Yeshua
Congregations in Israel and the diaspora
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/aut: Hebrew Bible and New Testament (Brit Hadashah); Jewish tradition valued in varying degrees.
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/sal: Salvation through Yeshua the Messiah, for Jew and Gentile.
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/sac: Immersion (mikveh) of believers; the Lord's Supper often linked with Passover.
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/esc: Premillennial, with a central place for Israel.
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/gov: Congregational with rabbis and elders; unions of congregations.
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/wor: Sabbath services with Torah reading, Hebrew prayers and Davidic dance.
traditions/messianic-judaism/profile/can: The Hebrew Bible and the New Testament.
traditions/church-of-south-india/summary: Formed on 27 September 1947 at St George's Cathedral, Madras, by the union of Anglican dioceses, the Methodist Church of South India and the South India United Church (Presbyterian and Congregational). It was the first union of episcopal and non-episcopal churches, accepting the historic episcopate while recognising existing ministries without reordination. It has been a leading voice for Dalit Christians, who form a majority of its members.
traditions/church-of-south-india/distinc: First union of episcopal and non-episcopal churches
CSI Liturgy (1950s) influential on liturgical renewal worldwide
Full communion with Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed
traditions/church-of-south-india/profile: Scripture as the supreme standard, with the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds.
Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
Baptism (infants and believers) and the Lord's Supper.
Episcopal-synodical: dioceses with bishops, a Synod and Moderator.
CSI liturgy and free forms in many Indian languages.
traditions/church-of-south-india/status: Active; one of the largest Protestant churches in India.
